The currently accepted age of the universe is **approximately 13.8 billion years**, with the most precise measurement from the Planck satellite (2018) giving **13.787 ± 0.020 billion years**.

This value is derived primarily from detailed observations of the **cosmic microwave background (CMB)** radiation— the afterglow of the Big Bang—combined with the ΛCDM (Lambda Cold Dark Matter) cosmological model. Key inputs include:

- The Hubble constant (H₀), measuring the current expansion rate (~67.4 km/s/Mpc from Planck),
- The densities of ordinary matter, dark matter, and dark energy,
- The geometry and composition of the universe, constrained by CMB anisotropies.

Independent methods—such as dating the oldest stars (e.g., in globular clusters) and measuring the expansion history using Type Ia supernovae and baryon acoustic oscillations—agree to within ~1% of this value, reinforcing its robustness.

So, while small refinements may continue with future data (e.g., from the James Webb Space Telescope or next-generation CMB experiments), **13.8 billion years** remains the standard, well-supported answer.
